title: WPMB/554/2024 of THAKURJI ENTERPRISES A PROPRIETORSHIP FIRM Vs STATE OF UTTARAKHAND

paras.text:
2024:UHC:9551-DB
UHIGH COURT OF UTTARAKHAND AT NAINITAL
HON'BLE THE ACTI NG CHI EF JUSTI CE SRI MANOJ KUMAR TI W ARI
AND
HON'BLE SRI JUSTI CE PANKAJ PUROHI T
UW r it Pet it ion ( M/ B) No. 5 5 4 of 2 0 2 4
U1 6 UPU
TH
UPU DECEMBER, 2 0 2 4
Thakurji Enterprises a proprietorship
Firm and Another --Petitioners
Ver su s
State of Uttarakhand and others --Respondent s
----------------------------------------------------------------------
UPresence: -
Mr. D.S. Patni, learned Senior Counsel assisted by Mr. Dharmendra
Barthwal, learned counsel for petitioners
Mrs. Mamta Bisht, learned Deputy Advocate General assisted by Mr.
S.S. Chaudhary, learned Brief Holder for the State of Uttarakhand
Mr. Sandeep Kothari, learned counsel for respondent No. 2.
Mr. Vikas Kumar Guglani, learned counsel for respondent No. 3
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Th e Cou r t m ad e t h e f ollow in g :
UJUDGMENT: U ( per Hon 'ble Th e Act in g Ch ief Ju st ice Sr i Man oj Ku m ar Tiw ar i)
1. Thakurji Enterprises is a proprietorship firm and
petitioner No. 2 is proprietor of the said firm. Petitioner
firm submitted bid in response to e-tender notice,
issued by Kum an Mandal Vikas Nigam Limited
(respondent No. 2), for operation of am usem ent park
and restaurant at lower station of ropeway, Mallital,
Nainital.
2. There were two other bidders, who submitted their
bid in response to the said e-tender notice. The
technical bids of petitioner firm and respondent No. 4
were declared to be non-responsive and technical bid of
1

2024:UHC:9551-DB
respondent No. 3 alone was declared to be responsive.
3. The sole ground for declaring technical bids of
petitioner and respondent No. 4 as non-responsive, is
that they have not submitted self-attested copy of GST
registration and only photocopy of GST registration was
supplied with the technical bid. Petitioners have
challenged the decision taken by the competent
authority, declaring their technical bid to be non-responsive.
4. Mr. D.S. Patni, learned Senior Counsel appearing
for petitioners submits that requirement of submitting
self-attested GST registration is to ensure that every
bidder is registered with GST department, and no
certificate is needed from any authority and, only the
bidders has to put his signature, which can be obtained
while opening the technical bids. He further submits
that it is not the allegation that petitioner firm is not
registered with GST departm ent and the only reason
for rejecting petitioner's technical bid is that he did not
submit self-attested GST registration. He submits that
requirement of submitting self-attested copy of GST
registration is a non essential or ancillary condition,
which can be waived. He relies upon judgm ent
rendered by Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of
Pod d ar St eel Cor p or at ion Vs. Gan esh En g in eer in g
W or k s an d ot h er s, reported in ( 1 9 9 1 ) 3 SCC 2 7 3 .
Para 6 of the said judgment is reproduced below: -
" 6 . I t is true that in submitting its tender accompanied by a
cheque of the Union Bank of I ndia and not of the State Bank
clause 6 of the tender notice was not obeyed literally, but the
question is as to whether the said non-compliance deprived the
Diesel Locomotive Works of the authority to accept the bid. As a
2

2024:UHC:9551-DB
matter of general proposition it cannot be held that an authority
inviting tenders is bound to give effect to every term mentioned
in the notice in meticulous detail, and is not entitled to waive
even a technical irregularity of little or no significance. The
requirements in a tender notice can be classified into two
categories - those which lay down the essential conditions of
eligibility and the others which are merely ancillary or subsidiary
with the main object to be achieved by the condition. I n the first
case the authority issuing the tender may be required to enforce
them rigidly. I n the other cases it must be open to the authority
to deviate from and not to insist upon the strict literal
compliance of the condition in appropriate cases. This aspect
was examined by this Court in C.J. Fernandez v. State of
Karnataka [ (1990) 2 SCC 488] a case dealing with tenders.
Although not in an entirely identical situation as the present
one, the observations in the judgment support our view. The
High Court has, in the impugned decision, relied upon Ram ana
Dayaram Shetty v. I nternational Airport Authority of
I ndia [ (1979) 3 SCC 489] but has failed to appreciate that the
reported case belonged to the first category where the strict
compliance of the condition could be insisted upon. The
authority in that case, by not insisting upon the requirement in
the tender notice which was an essential condition of eligibility,
bestowed a favour on one of the bidders, which amounted to
illegal discrim ination. The judgment indicates that the court
closely exam ined the nature of the condition which had been
relaxed and its impact before answering the question whether it
could have validly condoned the shortcoming in the tender in
question. This part of the judgment demonstrates the difference
between the two categories of the conditions discussed above.
However it remains to be seen as to which of the two clauses,
the present case belongs."
5. Learned Senior Counsel for petitioners also relies
upon judgment rendered by Hon'ble Suprem e Court in
the case of Har y an a St at e Coop er at iv e Su p p ly an d
Mar k et in g Feder at ion Lim it ed Vs. Jay am Tex t iles
an d An ot h er , reported in ( 2 0 1 4 ) 4 SCC 7 0 4 . Para 6
of said judgm ent is reproduced below: -
"6. Having heard the learned counsel for the parties and after
perusing the material on record, we find that adm ittedly
authorisation by the Board of Directors of the appellant
Federation was not placed before the courts below. But, we may
notice that a specific averment was made by the appellant
Federation before the learned Judicial Magistrate that the said
general power of attorney had been filed in connected case
being CC No. 1409 of 1995, which has neither been denied nor
disputed by the respondents. I n any case, in our opinion, if the
courts below were not satisfied, an opportunity ought to have
been granted to the appellant Federation to place the document
containing authorisation on record and prove the same in
accordance with law. This is so because procedural defects and
irregularities, which are curable, should not be allowed to defeat
substantive rights or to cause injustice. Procedure, a
3

2024:UHC:9551-DB
handmaiden to justice, should never be made a tool to deny
justice or perpetuate injustice, by any oppressive or punitive
use. (See Uday Shankar Triyar v. Ram Kalewar Prasad
Singh [ (2006) 1 SCC 75] ."
6. Per contra, Mr. Vikas Guglani, learned counsel
appearing for respondent No. 3, whose technical bid is
declared responsive, relies on judgment rendered by
Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of M/ s Agm at el
I n d ia Pv t . Lt d. Vs. M/ s Resou r sy s Telecom &
Ot h er s, reported in (2 0 2 2 ) 5 SCC 3 6 2 . Para 33 of the
said judgm ent is reproduced below: -
"33. Viewed from any angle, interference by the High Court in
this matter does not appear justified, particularly when no case
of mala fides or bias is alleged. Every decision of the
administrative authority which m ay not appear plausible to the
Court cannot, for that reason alone, be called arbitrary or
whimsical. The High Court, in the present matter has obviously
proceeded with an assumption that the view as being taken by
it, in acceptance of the case of the writ petitioner, was required
to be substituted in place of the views of the tender inviting
authority. That has been an error of law and cannot sustain itself
in view of the consistent binding decisions of this Court,
including the three-Judge Bench decision in Galaxy
Transport [ Galaxy Transport Agencies v. New J.K. Roadways,
Fleet Owners & Transport Contractors, (2021) 16 SCC 808 :
2020 SCC OnLine SC 1035] "
7. Law is well-settled that this Court while exercising
power of judicial review cannot substitute the view of
tender inviting authority and decision taken by him has
to be respected. However, judgm ent relied upon by
learned counsel appearing for respondent No. 3 is
distinguishable on facts. The question before this Court
is whether for non compliance of an ancillary condition
of tender notice, a bid otherwise responsive in each and
every aspect, can be rejected.
8. These days, State Departm ent or State owned
Corporations enter into different kinds of contract with
private entities; such contracts can be for procurement
4

2024:UHC:9551-DB
of goods/ m achines or for construction of road/ building
where contract is awarded to lowest bidder.
9. Bidding process is resorted to by State
departm ent/ corporations even while granting license
e.g., license for sale of liquor (both retail and
wholesale), mining, fishing etc., where contract is
awarded to the highest bidder.
10. I n both category of cases m entioned above, public
exchequer would be benefitted if m ore bidders
participate in the process. Rejection of bids for violation
of ancillary or non essential condition of notice inviting
tender on Standard Bidding Docum ent will have the
effect of reducing competition and this m ay adversely
affect public exchequer and also public interest. Thus,
power to reject technical bid for non com pliance of a
condition of Notice I nviting Tender/ Standard Bidding
Document (SBD), has to be exercised with
circumspection and in the best interest of State
departm ent/ corporation. Every non com pliance of some
condition of NI T/ SBD m ay not always result in rejection
of the bid and the nature of the condition alleged to
have been violated has to be considered by the
authority.
11. I n the present case, two bids out of three were
rejected only on the ground that certificate of GST
registration subm itted by bidders was not self-attested.
I t is not the case of em ployer that these bidders are
not registered with GST department. Since only lacuna
found in their technical bid is that GST registration
5

2024:UHC:9551-DB
submitted by them does not contain their signature and
such lacuna can easily be cured, therefore, rejection of
two bids out of three on the said ground alone does not
appear to be proper.
12. Mr. Sandeep Kothari, learned counsel appearing
for respondent No. 2 submits that he is not defending
the ground taken for rejecting technical bid of
petitioner.
13. After hearing learned counsel for the parties, we
are of the considered opinion that the condition of
submitting self-attested copy of GST registration is a
ancillary or non essential condition, therefore rejection
of petitioner's bid was not proper. Petitioner firm and
respondent No. 4, both had submitted copy of GST
registration, however only defect was that it was not
self-attested. I t is not the case where a certificate has
to be issued by som e authority, non furnishing whereof
would entail rejection of technical bid of the bidders.
Whether petitioner is registered with GST departm ent
can be easily verified from the concerned authority,
therefore, rejection of bids by taking hypes technical
view does not seem proper.
14. Here, the condition was of self-attestation and
petitioner and respondent no. 4 could have been asked
to put their signature on the copy of GST registration to
m ake it self-attested, even at a later point of time.
15. For the aforesaid reason, we allow the Writ
Petition. Order dated 03.12.2024, passed by com petent
authority whereby technical bid of petitioner was
6

2024:UHC:9551-DB
declared to be non-responsive, is set aside. The
technical bid subm itted by respondent No. 3 also shall
be reassessed and if only ground of rejection is non
furnishing of self-attested copy of GST registration,
then her technical bid shall also be declared to be
responsive. The Technical Evaluation Com mittee shall,
thereafter, proceed in the m atter, as per law.
